specPoints.text: understand reasons for the trends for Group 7 elements in: i melting and boiling temperatures and physical state at room temperature ii electronegativity iii reactivity down the group

primer.text: Descend Group 7 and everything shifts: colours deepen, boiling points climb, and the pull each atom exerts on electrons weakens. This note walks the ladder, explains volatility through intermolecular attractions, and shows why smaller halogens grab electrons - and react - more eagerly than their heavier cousins.

lessons.title: Appearance and volatility down Group 7
lessons.opening: The halogens are the Group 7 non-metals, and their look and their ease of evaporation both shift steadily as you descend. This lesson names the colour ladder, defines volatility through boiling point, and ties both trends to the growing electron clouds of the heavier atoms.
keyPoints: The Group 7 elements are the halogens, used as disinfectants, flame retardants and antiseptics.
Halogen colours darken steadily from fluorine through iodine going down the group.
Volatility means how readily a liquid evaporates, and a volatile substance boils low.
Melting and boiling points rise down the group, so volatility falls and iodine is the least volatile halogen.

low.restatement: Halogen colours deepen from pale fluorine to dark iodine, while boiling points climb, so the lightest halogen evaporates most easily and the heaviest least.
low.analogy: Think of a family of paints that darkens with every shade down the chart, and pots that get harder and harder to pour out as you move down.
low.examPointer: Quote the direction of both trends explicitly - darker colours and falling volatility down the group - because stating the direction earns the mark.

medium.restatement: Darkening colours and rising melting and boiling points both trace back to more electrons per molecule: bigger electron clouds give stronger induced dipole-dipole attractions that must be overcome to separate the simple molecular halogens.
medium.analogy: Heavier diatomic molecules are like stickier droplets - more contact area of weak attraction means more heat needed to shake them apart into gas.
medium.examPointer: Link colour depth and volatility to intermolecular attraction strength in one sentence when a question asks for an explanation, not just the observation.

check.stem: Which property increases steadily going down Group 7?

options.text: Melting point
options.explanation: Heavier halogens need more heat to overcome stronger intermolecular attractions, so their melting points climb.

options.text: Volatility
options.explanation: Higher boiling points mean evaporation happens less readily, so volatility falls rather than rises.

options.text: Electronegativity
options.explanation: Larger atoms attract bonding electrons more weakly, so electronegativity drops down the group.

options.text: Reactivity
options.explanation: Bigger atoms hold incoming electrons less strongly, so reactivity as oxidising agents falls.

check.stem: Why does iodine evaporate far less readily than fluorine?

options.text: Its diatomic molecules have many more electrons, strengthening the induced dipole-dipole attractions between them
options.explanation: More electrons per molecule means stronger London dispersion forces that must be supplied with heat to vaporise.

options.text: Iodine forms covalent networks that need breaking before it melts
options.explanation: Iodine is simple molecular, not a giant network, so no covalent lattice is disrupted on evaporation.

options.text: Iodine molecules are lighter and move more slowly
options.explanation: Iodine molecules are heavier, not lighter, and mass is not the direct cause here.

options.text: Iodine has a higher electronegativity that traps its electrons
options.explanation: Electronegativity decreases down the group, and it governs electron attraction in bonds, not evaporation.

check.stem: A volatile substance is best described as one that

options.text: Evaporates easily because it boils at a low temperature
options.explanation: Volatility describes ease of evaporation, which tracks a low boiling point.

options.text: Reacts vigorously with water to give an acid
options.explanation: That describes reactivity with water, not volatility.

options.text: Has strong forces inside its covalent molecules
options.explanation: Volatility depends on forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them.

options.text: Conducts electricity when molten
options.explanation: That is a property of ionic or metallic substances, irrelevant to volatility.

check.stem: Which set orders halogen colour correctly going down the group?

options.text: Pale yellow fluorine, yellow-green chlorine, red-brown bromine, dark grey-black iodine
options.explanation: The colours darken progressively from fluorine to iodine in this order.

options.text: Dark iodine, red-brown bromine, green chlorine, pale fluorine
options.explanation: That lists the group upwards, the reverse of the asked direction.

options.text: Green fluorine, yellow chlorine, orange bromine, silver iodine
options.explanation: These shades misassign the well-known halogen colours.

options.text: All halogens are colourless gases at room temperature
options.explanation: Halogens have distinct colours, and bromine is a liquid, iodine a solid.

check.stem: Bromine is used in flame retardants. Its room-temperature state and volatility compared with chlorine are

options.text: Liquid, and less volatile because its molecules attract each other more strongly
options.explanation: Bromine sits below chlorine, so its molecules carry more electrons, attract each other more, and it is the liquid halogen.

options.text: Gas, and more volatile because it is heavier
options.explanation: Bromine is a liquid at room temperature and heavier molecules are less volatile, not more.

options.text: Solid, and more volatile because it is dark coloured
options.explanation: Colour depth does not create volatility, and bromine is not solid.

options.text: Liquid, and more volatile because dark colours absorb heat
options.explanation: Absorbed colour has nothing to do with volatility; the intermolecular attraction decides it.

check.stem: Define volatility.
check.modelAnswer: Volatility is how easily a substance evaporates; a volatile substance has a low boiling point.

check.stem: State the trend in halogen colours down Group 7.
check.modelAnswer: The colours get darker going down the group, from pale fluorine through green chlorine and red-brown bromine to dark iodine.

check.stem: Explain why boiling points of the halogens rise down the group.
check.modelAnswer: Descending the group each diatomic molecule carries more electrons, so instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between the simple molecular halogens strengthen, and more energy is needed to separate the molecules into gas.

check.stem: A student spills liquid bromine and it soon fumes but the iodine crystals beside it barely change. Account for both observations.
check.modelAnswer: Bromine, with more electrons per molecule than chlorine but fewer than iodine, sits mid-ladder: volatile enough to fume at room temperature, while iodine's far stronger intermolecular attractions hold its molecules in the solid, so it sublimes only slowly.

lessons.title: Simple molecular structure and electronegativity
sourceHeadings: Trend in melting and boiling points
lessons.opening: Halogen crystals melt easily and the group's pull on bonding electrons fades as atoms grow. This lesson links both facts to structure: simple molecules held by weak induced dipole forces, and outer shells sinking ever further behind added screening layers.
keyPoints: Halogens are non-metals existing as diatomic molecules with simple molecular structures.
London dispersion forces between diatomic molecules are weak, explaining the group's low melting points.
Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts electrons in a covalent bond.
Electronegativity decreases down the group as atomic radius and shielding grow, so oxidising power also falls.

low.restatement: Each halogen is a pair of atoms joined covalently; between the pairs sit weak attractions, so little heat separates them. Larger halogens attract incoming electrons less because the outer shell sits further out behind more shielding.
low.analogy: Each molecule is a tiny magnet pair with weak glue between pairs; the bigger atoms are like magnets wrapped in extra foam, their pull felt less at the surface.
low.examPointer: Name the attraction as induced dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) and name shielding plus increasing atomic radius when explaining the electronegativity fall.

medium.restatement: Instantaneous electron imbalances in one non-polar molecule induce opposite dipoles in neighbours; more electrons make both the instantaneous and induced dipoles larger. The same growing radius and shielding that weaken electron capture also weaken electronegativity and oxidising ability.
medium.analogy: Crowded footballs flick neighbouring balls as they wobble; the bigger the ball's surface charge flicker, the stronger the flick it delivers.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish the two trends: melting/boiling rise because intermolecular force grows, while electronegativity and oxidising power fall because nuclear pull at the outer shell weakens.

check.stem: What structure do the halogens adopt at room temperature?

options.text: Simple molecular, as diatomic molecules with weak forces between the molecules
options.explanation: Halogen pairs are held covalently inside but only by induced dipole-induced dipole forces outside, the simple molecular pattern.

options.text: Giant covalent lattices of linked atoms
options.explanation: No covalent network joins different halogen molecules; each exists as a two-atom unit.

options.text: Giant ionic lattices of halide ions
options.explanation: The elements are neutral molecules, not ion arrays; halide ions appear in their compounds.

options.text: Metallic lattices with delocalised electrons
options.explanation: Halogens are non-metals; there are no delocalised electrons to carry charge.

check.stem: Electronegativity falls down Group 7 mainly because

options.text: Atomic radius and shielding increase, so the outer shell feels less nuclear attraction
options.explanation: Larger atoms hold their bonding electrons more weakly as distance and inner-shell screening grow.

options.text: Nuclear charge decreases as you go down the group
options.explanation: Nuclear charge actually rises with proton number; shielding outweighs it.

options.text: The molecules become diatomic and share electrons internally
options.explanation: Diatomicity is constant across the group and does not set electronegativity.

options.text: Electronegativity is constant because all halogens need one electron
options.explanation: The group shares valency, but electronegativity still varies with size.

check.stem: Which statement about oxidising power of the halogens is correct?

options.text: It decreases down the group, matching the fall in electronegativity
options.explanation: A weaker pull on incoming electrons makes each heavier halogen a poorer oxidising agent.

options.text: It increases down the group as atoms get heavier
options.explanation: Extra mass does not help electron capture; the pull weakens.

options.text: It stays constant because each halogen forms a 1- ion
options.explanation: Forming the same charge does not mean the same ease of gaining electrons.

options.text: It depends only on the melting point of the halogen
options.explanation: Melting point tracks intermolecular force, not electron capture.

check.stem: Why are the melting points of the halogens low compared with ionic substances?

options.text: Only weak induced dipole-induced dipole forces between molecules need overcoming
options.explanation: Melting separates whole molecules, so the weak intermolecular attractions set the low energy cost.

options.text: Covalent bonds inside each diatomic molecule are weak
options.explanation: The covalent X-X bonds are strong; melting never breaks them.

options.text: The molecules carry permanent charges that repel
options.explanation: Halogen molecules are neutral with only fleeting dipoles.

options.text: Halogen molecules cannot pack closely together
options.explanation: Packing is not the issue; the attraction strength is.

check.stem: An instantaneous dipole-induced dipole force arises when

options.text: A fleeting electron imbalance in one molecule induces a matching dipole in its neighbour
options.explanation: A momentary unequal electron distribution creates a dipole that polarises the nearby molecule, and the two attract.

options.text: A permanent dipole in one molecule aligns with another permanent dipole
options.explanation: That describes permanent dipole-dipole forces, not the induced type.

options.text: A hydrogen atom bridges two electronegative atoms
options.explanation: That is hydrogen bonding, a different intermolecular force.

options.text: Electrons are transferred completely between the two molecules
options.explanation: Full transfer is ionic bonding, not an intermolecular attraction.

check.stem: Define electronegativity.
check.modelAnswer: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent bond.

check.stem: State and explain the trend in oxidising power down Group 7.
check.modelAnswer: Oxidising power decreases down the group because atoms get larger, outer electrons sit further from the nucleus with more shielding, and the pull on an incoming electron weakens.

check.stem: Explain why fluorine is the most electronegative halogen.
check.modelAnswer: Fluorine is the smallest halogen, so its bonding electrons in a covalent bond, or an incoming electron, feel the least shielding and the shortest distance to a strongly positive nucleus, giving the strongest attraction.

check.stem: Predict, with reasons, whether astatine below iodine would be a stronger or weaker oxidising agent than iodine.
check.modelAnswer: Weaker: astatine atoms are larger still, so incoming electrons meet even more shielding and greater distance from the nucleus, reducing the pull that makes a halogen an oxidising agent.

lessons.title: Reactivity as oxidising agents and the hydrogen test
lessons.opening: A halogen atom normally ends up as a 1- ion, which makes every halogen an oxidising agent. This lesson follows that reduction, shows why the bigger atoms do it worse, and uses the hydrogen reaction as the vivid vigour test of the trend.
keyPoints: A reacting halogen atom gains one electron to form a 1- ion, so the halogen is reduced and acts as an oxidising agent.
The oxidation number falls from 0 to -1 when a halogen reacts to form its halide.
Larger halogen atoms attract the incoming electron less strongly, so reactivity decreases down the group.
Reactions with hydrogen gas become less vigorous down the group, giving the trend a visible demonstration.

low.restatement: Each halogen picks up one electron, dropping its oxidation number from 0 to -1; the smaller halogens do this eagerly, the larger ones reluctantly, and the hydrogen reactions slow down in step.
low.analogy: Small combs pick up paper crisply; larger, more shielded combs barely lift it - the halogens' electron capture weakens the same way.
low.examPointer: Write the half-equation X + e- -> X- and state the 0 to -1 oxidation-number fall when asked why halogens act as oxidising agents.

medium.restatement: Electron gain is reduction, so the halogen oxidises whatever supplies the electron. The gain is easiest when the incoming electron meets little shielding and short distance to the nucleus, so reactivity tracks electronegativity down the group, and the vigour with hydrogen demonstrates it.
medium.analogy: A narrow funnel pours quickly; a wide, foam-lined funnel slows every pour - added shells slow the electron's arrival just the same.
medium.examPointer: Link reactivity to oxidising power and quote the hydrogen-reaction trend as evidence in a 'describe and explain' answer.

check.stem: When chlorine reacts to form chloride, the oxidation number change is

options.text: 0 to -1, so chlorine is reduced
options.explanation: The neutral atom gains one electron, dropping its oxidation number by one unit into the halide.

options.text: -1 to 0, so chlorine is oxidised
options.explanation: That reverses the actual electron flow during halide formation.

options.text: 0 to +1, so chlorine is oxidised
options.explanation: Chlorine gains electrons here; it does not lose them to become positive.

options.text: +7 to -1, a seven-electron gain
options.explanation: That leap belongs to chlorine in oxyanions like chlorate(VII), not to the free element.

check.stem: Why does iodine react less vigorously than chlorine with metals?

options.text: Its larger atoms shield and distance the incoming electron from the nucleus, weakening the attraction
options.explanation: Poorer electron capture means weaker oxidising power and slower, less vigorous reactions.

options.text: Iodine molecules contain stronger covalent bonds that resist breaking
options.explanation: I-I is actually the weakest halogen-halogen bond; electron capture, not bond strength, limits reactivity.

options.text: Iodine has a smaller nuclear charge than chlorine
options.explanation: Iodine's nucleus is much more positively charged; shielding is what weakens the pull.

options.text: Iodide ions repel metal ions more strongly
options.explanation: Repulsion between products is not the mechanism of the trend.

check.stem: In the reaction of a halogen with hydrogen gas, the halogen acts as

options.text: An oxidising agent, because hydrogen's oxidation number rises from 0 to +1
options.explanation: The halogen takes hydrogen's electron, being reduced itself while oxidising hydrogen.

options.text: A reducing agent, because it donates electrons to hydrogen
options.explanation: The electron flow is towards the halogen, not away from it.

options.text: A catalyst, because it speeds hydrogen splitting without change
options.explanation: The halogen is consumed into the hydrogen halide product.

options.text: A spectator, because its oxidation number never changes
options.explanation: The halogen's oxidation number falls from 0 to -1.

check.stem: The reaction with hydrogen provides evidence for the reactivity trend because

options.text: The vigour of the reaction with hydrogen decreases steadily down the group
options.explanation: A visibly gentler reaction with each heavier halogen demonstrates the falling oxidising power.

options.text: All halogens react with hydrogen at identical rates
options.explanation: The whole point of the test is the graded vigour down the group.

options.text: Hydrogen chloride is the only product any halogen forms
options.explanation: Each halogen forms its own hydrogen halide HX.

options.text: Hydrogen oxidises each halogen in turn
options.explanation: The halogen is the oxidising agent in these reactions.

check.stem: Which half-equation matches the electron gain that turns a halogen atom into a halide?

options.explanation: Each of the two atoms gains one electron, so the molecule needs two electrons to form two bromides.

options.text: Br2 + e- -> Br2-
options.explanation: A single electron cannot convert the whole molecule; each atom takes one.
That loses electrons, the opposite of halogen reduction.
The product is two separate bromide ions, not a doubly charged molecule.

check.stem: State what happens to the oxidation number of a halogen when it reacts to form its halide ion.
check.modelAnswer: It falls from 0 to -1 as the atom gains one electron, so reduction has occurred.

check.stem: Explain why fluorine reacts more vigorously with hydrogen than iodine does.
check.modelAnswer: Fluorine attracts the incoming electron far more strongly because of its small size and low shielding, so its oxidising power and reaction vigour are greater than iodine's.

check.stem: Explain why halogens act as oxidising agents in reactions with metals.
check.modelAnswer: The halogen atom gains the electrons that the metal loses, so the halogen is reduced while oxidising the metal, which is the defining action of an oxidising agent.

check.stem: Sodium reacts far more violently with chlorine than with iodine. Predict the comparable vigour with bromine and justify the ordering.
check.modelAnswer: Bromine should sit between them: it oxidises sodium more readily than iodine but less readily than chlorine, because its electron capture is intermediate - larger than chlorine's yet stronger than iodine's.

glossary.definition: A Group 7 non-metal that exists as a diatomic simple molecular substance and readily gains one electron to form a halide ion.
The ease with which a substance evaporates, tracked by a low boiling point.
The weakest intermolecular attraction, arising when a fleeting electron imbalance in one molecule induces an opposite dipole in a neighbour.
The strength with which an atom attracts the shared electron pair in a covalent bond.
The ability of a species to take electrons from another species, oxidising it while being reduced itself.
